e. Historic Character and Project Architecture
The project area has an historic air to it. This can be seen in the street design, brick paved sidewalks, cartways, and architecture. These items are more suggestive of a turn of the century or Victorian atomosphere, rather than one of an earlier period, say ante-bellum or colonial. The architectural styles of the residential properties located in the interior of the project could be described as "Philadelphia Row." A small pocket of "Tudor" architecture is found in the northeastern part of the project.
Information obtained from the Harrisburg Historical Society and the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission indicates that there are no places or structures within the project area that are listed in the National Register of Historic Places. The nearest historical site listed in the "National Register" is the Walnut Street Bridge, located a few blocks south of the Project area. There are no known plans to place any project properties in the "Register" at this time.
f. Racial Character and Composition
The Project area contains few non-whites. Based on a survey conducted during the S and P stages of the application, only 65 non-white families were found to be living in the area. It must be noted that over 221 buildings were vacant at the time of the survey. Sixty-Five families represent 4% of the total residential population of the project. Vertually all of these non-white families were found in neighborhood area number 3 (see appendix) along Green and Penn Streets.
It is probable that the actual precentage is somewhat higher than the 4% indicated. This is based on a review of the percentage of non-whites in the Census tracts that overlay the approximate area of the project. The Census tract covering the southern end of the project, and additional business areas to the east, indicates 4.5 percent-about the same as the project survey. However, the second Census tract covering the remaining majority of the project, and parts of the Hamilton N.D.P. area, has a non-white population of 25 percent.
Counter to the theory that the percentage of non-whites in the project is much higher than 4 percent; say 10 or 15 percent, is the fact that no blacks are included in the relocation workload of individuals, and only a few black families are included in the family workload.
